title: Flourishing and Full Circle

segments.spoken_text:
Welcome to our final session, Flourishing and Full Circle. We're going to return to the students and questions you began with, and turn your thinking into a next step you can use.
Have your day-one setup, private My students card and partnership notes nearby. By the end of this session, you'll have one classroom change and one purposeful conversation with a family or student to take forward. We'll also make time for reflection, resources and feedback.
You don't need to carry away an unmanageable list. One thoughtful action, informed by the people involved and open to review, is a useful place to begin.

segments.spoken_text:
Belonging, capacity and joy bring the threads of today together. Keep all three in the picture when you consider whether a change is helping a student flourish.
Belonging means being recognised, included and able to participate as oneself. Capacity asks us to consider what the day costs, what it protects and what helps restore energy. Joy includes interests, connection and authentic expression.
These ideas connect our neurodiversity-affirming lens, our classroom design and our partnerships. We begin with the person, learn about their experience, and bring student, family and school knowledge into the decisions.
Look again at the day-one setup you developed in Session Four. It may reduce a barrier to participation. Could it also support belonging or joy? How might it affect what the day asks of the student? Remember the questions from Session Three: what costs, and what lightens?
Academic progress can be part of the picture, but it won't tell us everything about a student's experience. Quiet compliance or doing something without support is not, by itself, evidence of flourishing. Keep returning to the student, and to belonging, capacity and joy, as you judge what your change is making possible.

segments.spoken_text:
Let's bring the strongest ideas together at your table. Open page twenty-six of your Participant Guide.
Each person has about a minute to share the strongest thing they're taking back to school. Choose something that has stayed with you: an insight, a question or a practical change. You can draw on the gallery walk from Session Four as well as your own planning.
Then make a shared shortlist of three ideas from the table that are most worth spreading. For each idea, name who needs to hear it, and the meeting or moment where you could share it. Be as concrete as you can. A particular colleague and a particular opportunity will help you see what to do next.
The activity allows eight minutes altogether. If you're working independently, make your own shortlist and identify who you could discuss it with. Pause here to work through the activity, then resume for the next step.

Let's return to your shortlist. Check that each idea has somewhere to go: a person who needs to hear it, and a real opportunity to talk. If an idea still feels broad, add one example of what it could mean in practice.
You can keep the other ideas for later. For now, we're going to make your own next action specific enough to begin, and clear enough to review.

segments.spoken_text:
Turn to page twenty-seven, Start, Continue, Reconsider. Place your Session Four day-one setup beside it, especially your commitment on page twenty-one: ready for day one, my first step. Early habits tend to stay with you, so this is a useful time to choose them deliberately.
Under Start, choose a small strategy you can begin next week. It can be the same ready-for-day-one step you have been developing. If you don’t have your own class yet, choose a placement class or a school where you do regular relief. Under Continue, identify something today has confirmed you already do well. Under Reconsider, name an approach you would now look at differently.
For each, ask how you will know it worked, and what evidence will help you judge that. For your Start, these sentence stems may help: I will. The barrier or demand I am addressing is. I will notice. I need to consult. I will review this on.
Choose something within your influence. Keep the focus on the student's access, participation and experience. An action that depends on the student appearing less Autistic needs rethinking. Consider what you can change in the environment, task or response, and whose knowledge you need before or while you try it. Include the people on your asking list.
Allow eight minutes. This is your card. When you're ready, share one thing with someone at your table if you feel comfortable. Pause the video now, and we'll return to check the action.

segments.spoken_text:
Let's look once more at your Start. Is it small enough to begin? Does it name a barrier or demand you can act on? Have you identified when you'll consult the student, family or team, and when you'll review what happens?
Check the evidence you plan to notice. If the measure is simply that the student becomes quieter or complies more readily, look again. What will help you understand their access, participation and experience? Include their perspective in a way that works for them.
Keep the action small, testable and open to revision. Your Continue and Reconsider are useful alongside it: one recognises a practice worth sustaining, and the other keeps your learning open.

segments.spoken_text:
Now let's plan the next conversation, on page twenty-eight. Bring forward your Session Five bridge notes from page twenty-five, the opening question you wrote during The first two minutes on page twenty-four, and the process change you chose in the power-dynamics reflection on page twenty-three.
Choose one real conversation you can have within two weeks, with a student's family or with the student themselves. Begin by writing the purpose in one sentence. What do you need to understand? Leave room for their perspective to shape the conversation.
Plan what you'll share, beginning with a strength, what you'll ask specifically, and what you'll offer. Include how the student's communication and preferences will be heard. Write two open questions, and note what you will listen for.
Now write your opening sentence, word for word. Say it quietly to yourself if that helps you hear how it might land. Is it clear and respectful? Does it invite something you don't already know?
Name one possible shared next step, leaving room for the conversation to change it. Record how you'll follow up, and when, where and how the conversation will happen. Apply your process change to those arrangements. Use initials or roles in your workshop notes.
If this will be your first conversation of this kind, note who could help you prepare or join you: a mentor, stage or faculty leader, or support staff.
You have eight minutes for the full activity. Pause here to make your plan, then resume.

segments.spoken_text:
Take a final look at your conversation plan. Have you prepared to listen, as well as to speak? Does the plan leave something meaningful to decide together? Have you made a way for the student's own perspective to be included?
You can prepare your opening and your questions without scripting the other person's response. If new knowledge changes the next step you had in mind, the conversation is doing useful work.
Keep the time and follow-up visible in your plan. One classroom action and one conversation now connect what you've learned today to the people and setting where you will use it.

Return to page five of your Participant Guide, My starting point. Earlier, you wrote about what school is for and what you were curious about. Read your own words back.
Now turn to the final reflection on page twenty-nine. Where were you when we began? Where are you now? What's different in how you're thinking about the students you have in mind?
Take a little quiet time with those questions. Then write one sentence, just for yourself: what will you do differently in your teaching?
This reflection can stay private. There is no need to share it. The live workshop allows four minutes here. Pause the video for the time you need, then resume when you are ready.

segments.spoken_text:
What are you curious to learn more about next? Look back at your questions on page five. Which have been answered, and which have become more specific? Page thirty brings together pathways for continuing the learning.
Webinars and deeper sessions can help you explore topics such as Universal Design for Learning, executive functioning, sensory design and anxiety. The Online Community of Practice is intended as a place to keep talking with other educators. The Positive Partnerships website also provides resources for educators, families and students.
The particular webinar titles and dates, and the Community of Practice link, are still awaiting confirmation in these materials. Use the confirmed follow-up information from your workshop organiser when those details are available. The workshop plan also includes sharing photographs of wall work through that community; check the local arrangements for your group.
For now, choose the pathway that fits your next question. You can begin with the resources at positive partnerships dot com dot au. Today is a starting point for continued learning, reflection and partnership.

segments.spoken_text:
Thank you for your attention, questions and professional reflection throughout these sessions. Take your action card and conversation plan with you, along with the sentence you wrote in your final reflection.
Stay curious, and keep students at the centre. Take one thoughtful next step, include the people who hold relevant knowledge, and review what happens. Student voice, observation and partnership can help you refine a small change into something that makes a meaningful difference.
Use the resources and the confirmed follow-up arrangements from your workshop team to stay connected. You don't need to have every answer before you begin listening, asking a better question or changing something within your influence.
Good luck with your next steps, and thank you for the care you bring to this work.
